newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu vows Israeli settlement going up.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu vows Israeli settlement going up.

text.p: Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu met Jordan's king and talked to the Palestinian president on Sunday but vowed to break ground this week on a Jewish settlement that has angered both.

Asked if the bulldozers would move onto the hilltop site in Arab East Jerusalem during the next day or two, Netanyahu told a joint news conference with King Hussein: "I said that they would start this week. They will start this week."

"There is no change in our decision," Netanyahu said. "Friends can, as I said, agree and sometimes disagree. We understand the worries, the worry that exists on the Palestinian side and other sides. But we have taken our decision."

Netanyahu and the king, meeting for more than two hours at the prime minister's office, said they spoke by telephone to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat who had twice refused to receive Israeli government envoys during the last 10 days.
The Israeli leader said he hoped the conversation with the PLO leader in the self-ruled Gaza Strip would put Israel's dialogue with the Palestinians on a new footing.
"It was a constructive conversation and I hope that the results will speak for themselves," the king said.

Neither Netanyahu nor the king elaborated on the chat. But Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan, asked if there was an effort to get Netanyahu and Arafat together, told Reuters: "You can say that."

In a gesture to the Palestinians, Netanyahu said Israel would allow Arafat to fly into and out of the Gaza Strip airport of Dahanya and an agreement on that could be signed on Monday. Full operation of the airport is a still unresolved issue.

King Hussein flew to Israel to console families of seven schoolgirls slaughtered by one of his soldiers at the border last week and to defuse tensions with Netanyahu over a harsh letter he wrote to the prime minister last week.

The king's letter echoed Palestinian officials who had warned of bloodshed if Netanyahu went ahead with his unilateral plans to begin work on the 6,500 houses for Jews at the site known as Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic -- Har Homa to Israelis.

Netanyahu says the settlement reasserts an Israeli right to all of Jerusalem and insists Israeli-PLO peace deals do not bar the construction. Palestinians claim East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967, as the capital of a future state.

Israel's police chief Assaf Hefetz added his own warning on Sunday, saying police shared the fears and assessments of other Israeli security forces about the prospect of violence if the building project went ahead.
"Construction there could heat up the situation and lead to a deterioration in relations," Hefetz told Israel Radio.

Netanyahu sparked an outburst of violence last September when he punched open a new entrance to a tunnel near Islamic shrines in East Jerusalem. The bloodshed claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.

As it happens Monday -- the originally scheduled day of groundbreaking -- is also the day that Netanyahu and Arafat had agreed to launch negotiations on the future of Jerusalem and other tough "final-status" issues.
Negotiators on both sides said earlier on Sunday that no time and place had been set for starting those talks.
Israel's Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi raised tensions further on Saturday, warning Arafat he faced possible expulsion from Gaza, where he has ruled since 1994, should he launch a wave of unrest.

Hanegbi's counterpart in Arafat's Palestinian Authority, Freih Abu Medeen, cancelled a meeting with the Israeli minister over the remarks. Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said he regretted Hanegbi's comments.

King Hussein visited each of the families of the seven slain schoolgirls. "Your loss is my loss, my personal loss," the king told the parents of the late Sivan Fatihi, 13. Jordanian officials said the gunman acted alone.

The king and Netanyahu announced plans to establish a recreational site at the beauty spot where the killings took place -- a site in Jordan leased by Israel for farming under a 1994 peace treaty and nicknamed the "Island of Peace".
